Here's an interesting S. flava from Lexington Co, SC. The population here is supposedly S. flava var. rugelii, but perhaps the red throat isn't as pronounced on some clones such as the one below. Unfortunately, despite coming from a histically strong and decently big population, I've heard the population in the wild was recently damaged by beavers in the past few years. The status of these plants in the wild is unknown.

This is a relic population of S. flavas since it's pretty isolated and far away from "the main" flava populations in South Carolina. No doubt, these genetics are unique.


Anyhow, here's some photos, taken late April 2013:

Tony-not sure, as I've never been there. I've been told there's S. rubra ancestral and some interesting S. purpurea venosas that grow there as well. My understanding is this is an isolated population, distant from other populations.

Yuri-interestingly enough, most of the plants from this population are S. flava var. rugelii, but this clone seems to be closer to the maxima type as you pointed out.

posts.body_html:
I'm happy to report that I have found this population and it is thriving. I will post pics in a new thread when I get a chance. Var. rugelii and var flava were the most common, with a few var maxima scattered around as well. The purp venosa are unique, and there are some nice long-lidded (ancestral?) rubra. 

Pics posted: S. flava, rubra, and purpurea venosa in Lexington Co. SC
